spec.cue: The view is wide and soft, with a blurred middle and a faint violet tint where ultraviolet would show. Movement stands out and still things fade.

fov.note: Whole field of both eyes together, from a review figure of 270 degrees and a second general figure of about 300 degrees.

cpd.note: Honeybee worker resolution from the main compound eyes.

fovea.note: No record gives a magnification between the middle and the edge of the eye.

uvBlue.note: The app's choice for showing ultraviolet in the blue channel.

sat.note: Bees have three colour classes, so colour is kept, but the app's choice sets the strength.

gain.note: No whole-picture brightness advantage is cited for the main eyes.

gate.note: Still things are dimmed but not hidden, since the records show that bees see static patterns.

rate.note: The app's choice. The records give a bee flicker fusion near 200 hertz, against a person's 60, which would suggest about 0.3, but the app eases it to 0.5 for a softer view.

glow.note: The app's choice for how movement glows.

living.note: No record shows that bees pick out living movement.

topoA.note: No record gives a sharper middle for the main eyes.

BEE.note: Ultraviolet, blue and green peaks of the honeybee worker from one review table; the mapping follows the usual bee convention, UV shown as blue, blue as green, green as red.

rows: A honeybee sees about 0.26 cycles a degree at best, roughly 1 part in 230 of a person's detail. The view is soft for that reason.
Bees see nearly all around them, about 270 to 300 degrees across both eyes, with only a small blind patch behind and below.
Bees see ultraviolet, blue and green, and not red. Their three colour receptors peak near 346, 430 and 540 nanometres, so the view shows bee colours in place of ours.
Speed, tint and the app's own choices

The slower speed, the violet tint, the glow of movement and the fading of still things are the app's own choices. The records do not give their strength; a bee's flicker fusion near 200 hertz is the reason for the slower pace.

claims.how: Two review records give about 270 and about 300 degrees for the whole bee field; 270 is the value used, graded g because both records are from a wider or general group.
The review gives the honeybee worker's highest resolved spatial frequency as 0.26 cycles per degree.
Honeybee peaks from one review table: 346 nm for the UV class, 430 nm for blue and 540 nm for green.

quotes.quote: They found that the highest spatial frequency reliably resolved by the bees was 0.26 cycle deg−1, with no evidence of a difference in acuity between horizontal and vertical gratings.
a very coarse representation of the whole 270° bee eye horizontal field of view
Bees can see ~300° horizontally on the body plane with low spatial resolution for peripheral ommatidia
In contrast to us, bees can see UV light but not far red.
At ca. 200 Hz the FRC drops to 50%.
